metadata.title: The Arrow Points The Other Way
metadata.audience: students — smart people getting started with AI
metadata.note: ai-explainer chassis, claude-hai channel. Topic: quantum AI. The brief's central claim — that qubits find patterns in large classical data sets faster than ordinary computers — is the least supported part of the field, so the reel reports what is demonstrated instead: the arrow currently points from AI to quantum (AlphaQubit), classical-data loading is the bottleneck, and several claimed QML speedups were dequantized. The brief's drug-discovery and materials-science claims SURVIVE, and the reel says why they survive on principle. FRAMEWORK: WHICH DIRECTION / WHERE DOES THE DATA LIVE / DID A CLASSICAL ALGORITHM TRY. Every figure carries its source on screen — see SOURCES.md / FACTCHECK.md.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name. HAI short-form greeting.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane, and this week: quantum A I. There is something real here, and it is almost the opposite of the version you usually hear.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the week's question, answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the topic question and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "is quantum computing about to make AI dramatically better at finding patterns in data?"
props.segment: The Arrow Points The Other Way

where it does win: simulating matter

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — one breath, and it states the inversion up front
beats.narration_text: In one breath. The usual story is that qubits will find patterns in huge data sets faster than ordinary computers — weather, markets, supply chains. That claim is the weakest part of the field. The strongest result runs the other way: artificial intelligence is what is currently making quantum computers work. And the place quantum will genuinely win is not your data. It is chemistry.

shot.show: the expected direction quantum→AI, then the demonstrated direction AI→quantum
shot.visual_intent: Two labelled boxes, QUANTUM and AI. An arrow draws from QUANTUM to AI labelled 'the usual story' in ink, then fades back. A second arrow draws the other way, AI to QUANTUM, in terracotta, labelled 'what is demonstrated'. The reversal is the beat.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions, shown AS A STRUCTURE before any claim is examined
beats.narration_text: Three questions for any quantum A I claim. One: which way does the arrow point — is quantum helping A I, or is A I helping quantum? Two: where does the data live? Classical data has to be loaded into a quantum state, and that loading can cost more than the algorithm saves. Three: did anyone write a good classical algorithm and actually try? Ask those three, and most of the field sorts itself.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: WHICH DIRECTION / WHERE DOES THE DATA LIVE / DID CLASSICAL TRY
shot.visual_intent: Three cards land in a row, one per narration step. They stay on screen as the rubric every later beat is scored against.

beats.role_note: question 1 answered — the demonstrated result, with its measured numbers
beats.narration_text: Question one, and here is the demonstrated result. In twenty twenty-four, Google DeepMind published AlphaQubit in Nature — a transformer trained to decode errors inside a quantum processor. It beat tensor network decoding by six percent, and the widely used correlated matching by thirty. It held up from seventeen qubits to two hundred and forty-one. That is a real, measured, published win. And notice its direction: the neural network is helping the quantum computer, not the other way round.

shot.show: the two improvement figures and the qubit range, with the citation
shot.visual_intent: Two figures resolve as bordered results: 6% better than tensor network, 30% better than correlated matching. Beneath, the tested range 17 → 241 qubits. The direction label lands last in terracotta: AI → quantum. Source credits Nature 2024.

beats.role_note: question 2 answered — the loading bottleneck, which is exactly the brief's weather/markets claim
beats.narration_text: Question two. To find patterns in weather data with a quantum computer, the weather data has to get inside the machine — encoded into a quantum state, one load at a time. For a large classical data set, that preparation step can cost as much as the speedup buys. The algorithm is fast once the data is in. Getting it in is the problem, and it is the part the headline never mentions.
beats.new_visual_element: the load step, sitting between the data and the algorithm

shot.show: classical data, the encoding step, then the quantum algorithm — with the cost sitting on the middle stage
shot.visual_intent: Three boxes in a chain: CLASSICAL DATA → ENCODE INTO A QUANTUM STATE → QUANTUM ALGORITHM. The middle box is terracotta and widens as the cost lands on it. The outer two stay ink. The bottleneck is visibly in the middle, not at either end.

beats.role_note: question 3 answered — dequantization. The field's most useful correction.
beats.narration_text: Question three, and this is where the field got its most useful shock. In twenty eighteen an undergraduate, Ewin Tang, was asked to prove that a quantum recommendation algorithm had an exponential advantage. Instead, she wrote a classical algorithm that matched it. The speedup had not come from quantum-ness — it came from assumptions about the input. She and her co-authors went on to dequantize a whole class of quantum machine learning algorithms. Not all of them; topological data analysis resisted. But the lesson stuck: a claimed speedup that nobody has tried to beat classically is not yet a speedup.
beats.new_visual_element: the claimed gap, and what was left of it

shot.show: the claimed quantum-classical gap collapsing when a classical algorithm is written
shot.visual_intent: Two bars: QUANTUM short, CLASSICAL long — the claimed exponential gap. Then the classical bar contracts to match the quantum one, in terracotta, labelled 'dequantized'. A small note survives beside it: topological data analysis resisted. Source credits Tang, 2018 onward.

beats.role_note: where the advantage IS principled — and this is the half of the brief that survives
beats.narration_text: So where does quantum actually win? The case that has never been dequantized is simulating quantum systems — because the thing being simulated is itself quantum. Molecules. Reaction pathways. Materials. That is Feynman's original argument for building these machines at all, and it is why drug discovery and material science sit on almost every serious roadmap. Two of the four industries usually listed survive this. And they survive for a reason, not a hope.
beats.new_visual_element: which promised industries survive the three questions

shot.show: four commonly promised industries, two surviving and two not, with the reason
shot.visual_intent: Four rows: drug discovery and materials science resolve to ink with a tick and the reason 'the system being simulated is itself quantum'. Financial forecasting and supply chain stay hollow in terracotta, tagged 'classical data — see question 2'. Both halves held together.

beats.role_note: the timeline — and an honest caveat on the most-quoted benchmark in the field
beats.narration_text: And when? In twenty twenty-four Google's Willow chip, a hundred and five qubits, became the first to show error correction below threshold — errors shrinking as the machine grows. That is the milestone the field had waited for, and it is a milestone, not an arrival. Willow's headline benchmark, five minutes against ten to the twenty-five years, is random circuit sampling: a task chosen because it is hard for classical machines, not because anyone needs the answer. I B M's roadmap targets two hundred logical qubits in twenty twenty-nine and a thousand in the early thirties. Google says real-world problems need a million.
beats.new_visual_element: the roadmap, and what the famous benchmark actually is

shot.show: a dated roadmap from Willow 2024 to the million-qubit target, with the benchmark caveat called out
shot.visual_intent: A timeline with three dated stops: Willow 2024 below threshold; IBM 200 logical qubits 2029; 1,000 logical early 2030s. Beside it a terracotta caveat card on the famous 10^25-years figure: random circuit sampling, chosen to be hard, not useful. Source credits Nature and the published roadmaps.

beats.role_note: the rubric closed — all three questions scored, plus what to be excited about and what to doubt
beats.narration_text: Scored, then. Direction: the demonstrated wins today are A I improving quantum, not quantum improving A I. Data: for ordinary classical data, loading is the bottleneck — and that is exactly the weather-and-markets claim. Classical competition: assume someone will dequantize it, until someone has tried. Use this to be excited about the right thing, which is simulating matter. Be sceptical the moment somebody promises pattern-finding on your spreadsheet.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions scored, with what to believe and what to doubt

shot.show: the three question rows with their verdicts, then BE EXCITED / BE SCEPTICAL
shot.visual_intent: The three framework rows return and fill with verdicts. Beneath, two short lines: BE EXCITED ABOUT simulating matter; BE SCEPTICAL OF pattern-finding on classical data — the second in terracotta.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW + PROOF active-task rule — a scaffold with a good/bad discriminator
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Next time you meet a quantum A I claim, paste this. Which direction does this result run, is the data classical or quantum, and has anyone published a classical algorithm that tried to match it? A good answer names the direction and the classical baseline. A bad answer quotes a speedup with no baseline at all.
